title: Chapter 48 – Quiet Harvest
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Wenyuan]

The ledger says the clan has made a hundred and ten stones this month, and Wenyuan does not believe it.

He has checked the sum three times. He has checked it against Elder Aunt Wenjun's tally, and against the receipts from the Willow Ford market, and against the weight of the strongbox in the treasury, which he lifted himself, with both hands, on a night when he could not sleep. The numbers agree. They have agreed for six weeks. Spirit-iron ingots at forty stones the dozen, from Hu's refinery in the granary, to the market warden. Heartleaf salve at six stones the jar. A cartload of the clan's old black slate, ground fine, to a mason who wants it for ink. And, since the thaw, small and regular and impossible to trace, a trickle of pills.

Marrow Wash, Level One, medium grade. Blood Seal, Level One, medium grade. They come up out of the granary in clay bottles, three at a time, and Hu sells them by the dozen to a dealer at the Ford who asks no questions. A hundred and forty stones, Tally's satchel was worth. In a month the clan has already made more.

It is a very good month, Wenyuan thinks. He sets down his brush. It is the best month in four years. I should be glad.

He is not glad. He has been the Patriarch of Green Pine Hill for two hundred and twelve days, and he has learned one thing about the office, which is that when a house starts to prosper without a reason, the reason is always coming.

* * *

It is a small pleasant spring evening, and the study window is open. Down in the lower garden someone is raking last year's leaves. The air smells of cut grass and wet clay. On the desk before him lies the thing he has been trying to avoid reading for an hour, a letter from the Outer Court, in the neat round hand of Inspector Cheng Yun, which says, in four courteous lines, that the Inspector will return in the second week of summer to complete his audit.

Complete. He turns the word over. It is a very pleasant word for a man who has already found the deed fiber.

There is a knock at the door.

"Come."

It is his wife. She enters without hurry, in her plain gray gown with her hair tied up in the sensible knot she wears for the stillroom, and closes the door behind her, and, which she does not usually do, turns the key.

Wenyuan watches this with the first small cold touch of alarm.

"Qinghe."

"You have not been sleeping," she says. "You have been up at the treasury. You have counted the strongbox." She crosses the room and sits on the corner of his desk, lightly, with her hands in her lap. She has never in twenty years sat on his desk. "I would like to tell you not to worry. I cannot. I would like instead to ask you to come for a walk with me. It will take a few hours. You will need a cloak, and a lamp, and I would ask you not to ask me where."

"Is it Jian?"

"It is Jian. It is not bad." She tilts her head. "It is very large."

He looks at her. He has been married to her for nineteen years, and has known her for twenty-two, since the autumn she came up the river road with a bundle on her back and a bucket of dried herbs, and sat down in his father's courtyard and said that she did not require anything except permission to stay. In all that time she has asked him for exactly four favors. This is the fifth.

"Now?"

"After dark."

He stands. He takes down his cloak. "Then we shall go after dark," says Wenyuan, "and you will tell me as much as you are able on the way, and I will try very hard not to have the heart attack I have been expecting since midsummer."

"That is all I ask."

She smiles. It is a small, tight, remarkable smile, and he sees, with a lurch of the heart, that she is frightened. She is more frightened than she was at the Narrows.

* * *

They go up through the pines in the last of the light.

It is not the way to the quarry. He realizes that by the second turn. They go round it, by a deer path he has not walked since boyhood, along the east shoulder of the hill and down into a hollow of old hemlock where the ground is soft and the dark comes early. Here Jian is waiting.

He is sitting on a stump with his hands round his knees, in a gray hooded cloak that Wenyuan does not recognize. He has grown. It is a ridiculous thing to notice, in the dusk, in the middle of a forest. But the boy has grown, in the three weeks since the Narrows, as if he had been drinking spring water by the bucket, an inch at the least. His face has lost a little of its childish roundness. There is a ring round his eyes, very faint, very thin, a kind of pale gold, that catches the last of the daylight when he turns his head.

"Father," says Jian, and rises, and bows.

"Son."

They look at each other. Wenyuan has had a great many conversations with this boy, in two years, and has understood very few of them. It is the habit of the child to say the least that will do. It is the habit of the father to wait for the rest.

"I am going to show you something," says Jian. "I would like you to promise me three things first."

"I may refuse."

"You may." The boy's voice is quite steady. "The first is that you will not tell Uncle Wenshi, or Elder Aunt, or anyone. Not for a year. Not even Hu."

"Why Hu?"

"Because the Blood Shadow will ask him. And he will not be able to lie. Not for a thing that large."

Wenyuan looks at his wife. She nods, once.

"The second?"

"That you will not touch anything. Anything at all, without asking. Not a leaf. Not a stone." The faint gold ring shivers. "It will want you to. It is very polite about it. I think it is, in its way, lonely."

"And the third?"

"That you will let me say what I think it is, before you say what you think it should be used for." A very small pause. "Because I have thought about it for a month, and I have not yet thought of anything that is not going to cost somebody."

Wenyuan is silent for a moment.

"I promise," he says.

"All three?"

"All three."

The boy nods, as if a ledger has been balanced. He puts two fingers into his collar, and something small and pale and scaled looks out, with round black eyes, and sneezes.

"Father," says Jian, "this is Pebble."

* * *

He does not scream. He thinks about it afterward, with some pride.

The seam opens at the foot of a hemlock, with no more fuss than a curtain being drawn, a vertical line of green light the height of a man. It hums. A gust of cold wet air comes out of it, smelling of earth and rain, and Wenyuan, who has been a talisman drawer all his life and knows the feel of a spatial formation the way a blind man knows his own front door, feels the hair rise on his arms.

"It is not a talisman," he says, hoarsely.

"No."

"It is not a formation either." He puts out a hand and stops, an inch short. "It is a tear. It is a living tear. I have read of this. In my father's study, in the Founder's notes, there is a word for it. Seam. And a warning." He swallows. "That a hundred and nine men have died in the attempt to use one, and only a handful of those who walked through came out, and that the survivors would not say what they had seen."

"I know," says Jian. "I have been through it four times."

"Four times."

"Pebble walks it. I walk behind her." The boy glances at his mother, who has not moved. "Mother has been through twice."

Wenyuan turns, slowly, and looks at his wife.

She meets his eye. "I would have told you earlier," she says. "I wanted it to be a thing I understood first. I did not, and I do not, and I find I would rather you saw than that I explained."

He draws a long, slow breath. He lets it out.

"Show me," says Wenyuan.

* * *

The Orchard takes his breath away, and then, a moment afterward, gives it back.

He stands on the moss, in the pearly light, with the green haze stirring round his ankles, and the high stone vault of the ceiling soaring away above him like the roof of the world. There are rows and rows of dark, broad-leafed plants. There is a pool, a long way off, shining like a plate of green glass. There is a great silence, and in it a hum, so faint he feels it more in his teeth than his ears, of something old and patient and wholly without malice, waking up.

He does not speak for a quarter of an hour.

His wife has taken his hand. He has not noticed. He is looking at the nearest bed, at a tall tangle of silver-gray leaves with small white berries like pearls, and he is thinking, with the calm and perfect clarity that comes to a man at the exact moment the world has ended, that it is Heartroot. There are, by his count, forty plants in that one bed. It is the herb that the Southern Pavilion of Red Ridge imports, a sack a year, at ten stones the leaf. It is the herb that his father used to say could mend a broken meridian, if a man could ever afford the quantity.

"Wenyuan," Qinghe says gently.

"I am here."

"You are shaking."

"Yes." He looks down. It is true. His hand, the one the Sect crushed long ago, and which Qinghe's herbs have patched back to something like service, is trembling in hers like a leaf. "I am not afraid. It is simply that my father spent forty years looking for this. And he died not knowing it was under his feet."

"I think," says Jian, "that he did know."

Wenyuan turns.

The boy is standing at the edge of the moss with the pangolin at his shoulder, and his thin face is quite serious. "The note in the ledger," he says. "The last page. Look at the quarry spoil heaps. Ask the boy's teacher. You said the spoil heaps were slag. They were. But I think Grandfather did not mean the slag. I think he meant the quarry. He knew the Founder's notes. He knew there was a thing under the hill, and he knew it would answer someone, and he did not know who." The boy's mouth moves, very slightly. "I think he thought it would be Hu."

"Why Hu?"

"Because Hu is a seam-man. Of metal. In his way. He sees the gap in a weave." A pause. "He did not know a seamwalker could be a beast."

For a long moment Wenyuan says nothing. In the glimmering hush, a single moth drifts down between them and settles on the Patriarch's sleeve, and sits there, breathing, as if it had known him all its life.

Father, he thinks. You old fox. You wrote me a riddle with your last breath, and you left me to solve it on my knees.

He finds, to his surprise, that he is laughing.

* * *

They show him the rest.

The pool, which Jian calls the reservoir, and which hums when Wenyuan's hand passes over its rim. The terrace and the lock plate, which Wenyuan stares at for a long time without a word. It is, he says at last, a cousin of the fortieth step. It is a younger daughter of the same hand. He kneels, and runs his fingers over the fine black lines, and says very quietly, in the voice of a man reading a letter from someone who has been dead for a thousand years, "Whoever made this was better than any of us."

The Wardens, eleven of them, standing in their loose ring on the moss. The gate-Warden is the last to move. It stands in front of the Patriarch, vast and black, with its granite shield and its amber lamp, and for a long moment seems to consider whether he is a thing to be allowed.

It says you smell like your boy, Pebble translates, a little drily. It says that will do.

"I am relieved," says Wenyuan.

The Bell, in its reeds. The herb beds. The half scroll of the Seed Canon, which Jian has copied and hidden, and which Wenyuan reads in the green light with his brows drawn down.

"Five-element," he says.

"Yes."

"It is a method for the five-element root. Not a patch. A Canon." He looks up. For a moment, in the dim, he looks a great deal younger. "Jian, there is no such thing. I have studied in three libraries. They all say the same. A five-element root is a flaw. It is the commonest curse of the pseudo-roots. No clan has ever bothered with a Canon for it, because there is not a single recorded case of a five-element child who reached the Foundation stage."

"There is one," says Jian, mildly.

Wenyuan stares at him. Then, very slowly, he begins to understand. He looks at the boy's face, at the pale gold ring round the dark of his eyes, at the quiet calm in him, at the small old watchfulness in the way he stands. He looks at his height.

"You are an eighth-stage," says Wenyuan, in a very odd voice.

"Early."

"At ten."

"Yes."

"Qinghe, did you know?"

"I guessed." She is very pale. "I did not guess the stage."

"I see." The Patriarch sits down, quite suddenly, on the edge of the moss. He is silent for a time, with his hands hanging between his knees. "I have been walking about this hill, for a year, being very careful not to ask what you are. I had thought, I think, that if I did not ask, it would not become true." A thin, unsteady laugh. "I find now that it was true all along, and that the only thing I had succeeded in doing was to be the last to know."

Jian does not answer. He has gone, in the light, very still, and Pebble has crept down his arm and into his cupped hand, and is looking up at the Patriarch with her small bright eyes.

"I am not angry," says Wenyuan.

"I did not think you would be."

"I am frightened. It is different." He lifts his head. "Tell me what it costs."

* * *

So Jian tells him.

He tells it with a flat, dry precision, like a clerk reading out an inventory, in the green dusk by the pool. The scales that Pebble loses with each seam. The tithe of the Seed. The old drinking of the vein, through the dry roots of the Orchard, a quarter-inch a year for four hundred years. The tracker's hound, and the dying woman, and the promise he made. He tells it all, in order, without a break. When he comes to the part about Mei Ru, he stops, once, and goes on.

Wenyuan hears him out. When it is over, the Patriarch sits for a long while with his chin on his fist.

"There is a fourth cost," he says at last.

"Sir?"

"The one you have not named. The one that is mine." The thin tired face is calm. "It is that we shall have to lie. For a year. To a clan that trusts us. To Wenshi, who is my brother. To Hu, who is, I begin to think, the only man alive who would understand every word of this. To every child on the hill who asks where the herbs come from." He closes his eyes. "I have never in my life told a lie that mattered. I find I am about to tell several hundred."

"Father—"

"No. Listen. I do not say it to be pitied. I say it because you were right to put the question first." He opens his eyes. "A thing like this is not a treasure. It is a duty, with a bad smell. It will be the death of us if we use it badly, and the death of the clan if we do not use it at all." His mouth tightens. "I will keep it. I will keep it, I think, for exactly as long as it takes to keep the Blood Shadow from learning that it exists. And then I shall have to decide."

"Decide what?"

"What to do with fifty plants of Heartroot and a mountain that is drinking itself."

He rises. He is stiff. His knees crack. He is, he thinks, forty-six years old, and a Patriarch for two hundred and twelve days, and a man who has known for a single hour that his youngest son is an eighth-stage cultivator with a seed in his belly and a talking beast in his sleeve. He looks, for the first time in nine months, entirely sane.

"The third restoration," he says. "Qinghe. You said you had a recipe."

"I have." His wife's eyes are bright. "It wants frostbell, and mourner's cup, and a heartroot leaf, fresh, in the first hour after plucking. Third Aunt's frostbell would not do it. I had thought we might have to wait another year, for the Pavilion to sell us a sack." A small, tremulous smile. "I had not thought we should have it here."

"Then brew it."

"Tonight?"

"Tonight." Wenyuan looks at the quiet beds, and the soft glimmering pool, and the great black-shouldered Warden standing at his post. He looks at his son. And he does a thing he has not done in years, which is to put out his hand, and lay it, very lightly, on the boy's head.

"Thank you," he says, "for telling me."

Pebble sneezes again. It is a small ridiculous sound, and in the green hush of the Orchard it carries a long way. And somewhere across the pool, in the dim, a small lame Warden shuffles a half-step forward, and bows.

* * *

They brew it in the Orchard, by the pool, in a small iron pot that Qinghe has carried in her bundle.

It takes three hours. She works with a grave, quick, unhurried skill that Wenyuan has watched for twenty years and has never quite understood. She does not measure. She knows. The frostbell goes in first, bruised in a stone bowl, and then the mourner's cup, flower and stem; the water comes from the pool, drawn in a dipper, and is so clear and so cold that it makes the iron sing. The Heartroot is last. Jian plucks it, one silver-gray leaf, with a pair of tweezers, and carries it across the moss on a square of white cloth as if it were a bird's egg.

"Now," says Qinghe.

The leaf goes in. The pot hisses. A cloud of pale gold vapor rolls up, smelling of cut grass and snow, and Wenyuan, who has not wept at his father's funeral nor at his brother's, finds his eyes are wet.

A third restoration, he thinks. Three years of saving. Three years of buying one sack, one season, with the clan's grain money. And here it is, in an hour, out of a puddle.

"Drink it hot," she says. "In three swallows. It will not be pleasant."

"I did not suppose it would be."

It is not pleasant. It is like swallowing a lit lamp. The warmth goes down his throat in a bright thread and opens, in his chest, in his belly, in the long scarred roads of his channels, where for nine years there has been a thin dry cold like the draft under a door. He feels each of them wake. He feels the old broken place in the right arm, the one the Sect left him, spark and burn and knit. His whole body arches. He bites down on a groan.

"Breathe," says his wife, kneeling beside him, with both her hands pressed flat to his back. "Breathe. Slowly. It is only the Qi rushing in. Let it."

He lets it.

When he comes to himself he is lying on the moss, with his head in her lap, and the green vault is a long way above. He is soaked with sweat. His hands are shaking, but not from weakness. It is a clean, bright, restless trembling, like a horse that has been too long in the stable.

"How do you feel?" says Jian, from somewhere near.

"Old," says Wenyuan, honestly. "And a good deal less so than I did."

He sits up. He opens his hand, and a small bead of white light, no bigger than a grain of rice, forms in the middle of the palm and rolls round it, once, steadily. It is a thing he has not been able to do in nine years without a talisman.

Sixth of ten, he thinks. Sixty-one parts in a hundred of what I was. Another two brews, and I shall be as I was at thirty.

It is not a thing he can say aloud. He looks at his wife and son, in the half dark, with the pool glimmering behind them and the Wardens standing in their ring, and finds that he has no words at all. In the end he says the only one that fits.

"Well."

Qinghe laughs, a low shaken sound. Pebble, who has crept across the moss and sat on Wenyuan's knee, looks up into his face with grave round eyes, and he feels, quite distinctly, in the back of his mind, a small warm brush of attention, a flicker of curiosity, like the touch of a feather. It is not a voice. It is a feeling, and he knows what it says as well as if it had spoken.

Friend, says the feeling. Good smell.

"I am honored," says Wenyuan, gravely. "Madam Pebble."

* * *

They come out at midnight, by the Bell, into a quarry washed white by the moon.

The seam folds shut behind them with a sound like a sigh. The wind is cold. Below them, the whole of Green Pine Hill lies sleeping, the terraces black and silver, the roofs of the hall and the schoolhouse and the granary dim under their tiles. Somewhere a dog barks, once. A single lantern burns in the window of the gatehouse, where the night guard keeps his watch.

Wenyuan stands on the lip of the quarry, with the wind in his gray hair, and looks at it for a long time.

"They will ask," he says. "Where the money comes from."

"The ledger says Hu's refinery," says Qinghe. "The Ford says Hu's refinery. Elder Aunt believes it, because she has not seen a single reason not to."

"Cheng Yun will not." The Patriarch's voice is quiet. "He will come in the second week of summer. He will look at the strongbox. And he will look at the vein, which Third Aunt tells me is still falling, and he will say, in that careful gentle voice, Patriarch, you have a hill that grows poorer every month, and a treasury that grows richer. And then he will wait." He looks down. "I do not know what I shall say."

"The truth," says Jian, "a little at a time."

"Which truth?"

"That Hu is better than anyone knew." The boy has his hands in his sleeves. "It is not a lie. He is. He has been making spirit-iron out of slag for four months. He has been making it better than the Sect's own refiners, and he did it with one arm and a broken rod. If you tell Cheng Yun that the clan has hired a master, he will want to meet him. And he will find a drunk, and a very great artisan, and a man who has no idea where the herbs come from."

Wenyuan looks at him.

"You have thought about this."

"For a month."

"Hm." The Patriarch folds his arms. "I find I am a little afraid of you. I find also that I am very proud, which is a most inconvenient combination."

"Yes, Father."

"Come home. Both of you. I shall sit up tonight with my father's riddle, and see what else he left me." He turns toward the dark roofs of the hall, and then pauses. "Jian."

"Sir?"

"What will you do with the Seed? The second half."

The boy considers. "Find it," he says. "I think someone has it. The other half. And I think the Blood Shadow wants it too." A small, odd pause. "Mei Ru said, everything they want is under a pool."

Wenyuan's breath catches. In the white light of the quarry he stands very still, and then, slowly, as if the thought has come to him from a very long way off, he turns and looks east, toward the black ridge beyond the river, where the Sect's old inn stands at Three Willows, and the cold lights of the Blood Shadow's border posts are burning in the dark.

"Then we shall have to be the first to look," says the Patriarch.
